segments: A gym wall at six in the morning,
green paint, white block letters tall
as a door:
if you quit once, it becomes a habit.
Never quit.
Nobody signed it, nobody dated it, and
nobody has ever taken it down for review.
Everything else in that building gets
audited -
the fire code gets inspected every
spring, and the locker prices get
argued about at the front desk.
But the one rule about what we should
all do with our whole lives just hangs
there, and we nod at it, every single
day, on our way to somewhere else,
and we never once ask who wrote it.
It's the only contract we all honor
that nobody ever signed.
The rule has exactly one job, and
you've felt it do that job.
The job is a hand on your shoulder.
Here's a man at a kitchen table, coat
still on, holding three pieces of
paper in two closed hands.
A lease on a shop that hasn't paid for
its own lights in two years.
A ticket for a show tonight, bought
back in October by a slightly different man.
A schedule for a league he stopped
loving two seasons ago.
He wants something small, the way
people usually do:
he wants to put one of them down. Just one.
And the hands won't open, and we
should say this clearly before anything else -
he's not weak, and he's not a fool,
and neither are you.
If you've ever held something two
years past the wanting, you already know him -
most of us are him.
He keeps the shop open to protect the
money he's already lost, and tells
people it's about to turn a corner.
It's been about to turn that corner so
long it has a permanent address there.
That's not a business plan.
That's a hostage negotiation
where he's both parties.
Now, about the wall's author.
The quote belongs to Michael Jordan,
and the record keeper would like a
word, because he retired three times -
October 1993, January 1999, and
finally in 2003, after a last season
in Washington.
Three quits, spread across a decade,
and here's the part that matters to us:
every one of them was reasonable.
He left when leaving made sense,
he came back when coming back made
sense, and his life is fine.
The man kept deciding, over and over,
in public.
The quote never checked in with its
own author.
Nobody repaints a wall just because
the author changed his mind.
A banquet hall with balloons and a
banner over the door.
We throw a party for every start we
can find, don't we - the new job, the
new house, the new marriage, the new city.
And we're right to, because starts are
worth the cake.
But look at the guest list, because
every one of those starts required a
quit that nobody catered.
She left a firm to open the food truck.
He left a hometown to take the job.
Every start we've ever celebrated is a
quit wearing a better outfit.
Starting and quitting are the same door,
photographed from opposite sides -
we frame one picture and hide the
other in a drawer.
We cheer every entrance, and we bill
every exit.
Half the guests at every wedding are
toasting somebody's excellent divorce.
So why won't his hands open - his, and
ours - if the wanting is real?
Because somebody weighed the grip.
A grocery scale with a thumb resting
quietly on it - that's your head,
and two psychologists named Kahneman
and Tversky
spent years measuring the thumb.
Losses weigh more than gains, reliably
and by a lot:
in their 1992 numbers the tilt came
out near two and a quarter to one.
Lose a hundred dollars, and you need
about two hundred and twenty-five in
wins before you feel even.
One honest footnote:
researchers still argue over that
exact figure,
though the tilt itself keeps showing
up in every version of us they test.
And the tilt is the whole point.
Leaving anything is priced, before
you've weighed a single fact about
your actual life,
at more than double what staying costs.
The game was set before any of us sat down.
Your brain is a casino
that rigged the odds against leaving.
And you're a regular.
A theatre ticket on a dashboard, and
outside the windscreen, a snowstorm.
In 1985, Arkes and Blumer ran the
theater-ticket experiments, and the
finding has a terrible little smile on it:
people who paid more for their tickets
went to more of the shows -
even when going made their evening
measurably worse.
The money was gone either way.
It left when the ticket was bought,
and some part of you always knows it.
But the ticket in the coat pocket has
a small voice, and the voice has a
four-word speech:
you already paid.
That speech works in theatres, and it
works in our marriages, and our
careers, and it has worked in our wars.
"You already paid" is the only ghost
story money knows how to tell.
And we keep driving into the snow to
hear the ending.
Economists call it the sunk-cost fallacy.
The theatre calls it a subscription.
A donkey in an empty field, standing
exactly between a bale of hay and a
pail of water.
Equally hungry, equally thirsty, the
two prizes equally far - that's the trap.
The setup is seven hundred years old,
aimed at a philosopher called Jean
Buridan, with older versions in
Aristotle and Al-Ghazali,
so this donkey has excellent references.
Unable to find one reason to prefer
the hay over the water,
it declines to choose at all, and it
dies of both.
Read that outcome carefully, because
the donkey didn't die of hunger, and
it didn't die of thirst.
It died of the standing still.
And we owe the animal an apology of
sorts, because it wasn't being
stubborn - it was being safe, and as
long as it never chose, it could never
choose wrong.
Seven centuries of philosophers have
handled the case and reached a rare
unanimous verdict:
refusing to choose is a choice,
and it's the one with the worst record
in the file.
The debate continues, as debates do.
The donkey remains dead.
A textbook open to a page of hexagons
- which is what dread looks like in a
chemistry building - and beside it, an
ashtray.
Some hard stretches are tunnels:
dark, long, miserable,
and attached to daylight at the far end.
Every doctor you've ever trusted got
through organic chemistry,
which proves the far end exists.
Other hard stretches are holes wearing
a tunnel's uniform.
Nobody has ever smoked their way
through emphysema,
because that road doesn't go anywhere;
it just goes down.
From the inside, the two feel identical -
both hurt, both invite you to stop,
and both come with a voice saying
winners don't.
The wall can't tell them apart for us,
because the wall only knows one word.
It says push to the medical student
and the smoker alike.
A rule with one answer for two
different roads isn't wisdom. It's paint.
Knowing which one you're in is the
entire skill.
Let's say that again, slowly, because
it isn't a joke.
Knowing which one you're in is the
entire skill - and there is one quit
that always, without exception, puts
you in the hole.
A plant on a windowsill in
Connecticut, 1976.
Ellen Langer and Judith Rodin ran a
study across two floors of a nursing home.
On one floor, residents were given a
plant to care for themselves, along
with small daily choices - how to
arrange the room, which night to see the film.
On the other floor, the staff handled
everything, kindly and completely,
plant included.
Eighteen months later, the researchers
counted.
On the floor where everything was
handled, thirty percent of the
residents had died.
On the floor where the residents kept
deciding, fifteen percent.
Those are the numbers as the study
reported them, and the literature has
raised its caveats since -
but the plain reading deserves a plain
sentence.
The people who kept making small
choices died at half the rate.
The plant was never the medicine.
The choosing was.
So there is exactly one quit in our
whole story
that can cost you everything,
and it isn't the lease,
and it isn't the league,
and it isn't the show.
It's quitting the deciding.
Snow on a front step, and the man
standing in it, ticket in hand, one
hour before curtain.
He doesn't want to go,
and for the first time in years
he lets the wanting count as evidence.
Watch his hands now, because they're
about to do the bravest small thing
you'll see all week.
He bends down and lays the ticket on
the step -
face up, paid for, finished.
Nothing dramatic follows,
which is how most of our bravest moments go.
The ceiling holds, the floor stays put,
the world declines to end.
And his hands are open, for the first
time all evening,
and maybe for the first time in years.
Here's what the wall never told him,
and never told you either:
open hands aren't empty hands.
They're available ones.
He goes inside,
and the last thing you see is what the
open hands pick up - a small plant,
lifted onto the windowsill, into the
light, his to keep alive from now on.
Because there really is one thing we
never quit, and it was never the
lease, or the league, or the ticket.
It's the deciding, and tonight he did
it, on a cold step.
That isn't giving up.
That's the grip, finally letting go of him.
The wall will still be there tomorrow,
freshly painted, two words long.
Let it say what it wants -
we can afford to be generous with it now.
It was never the wall's decision to make.
